## Overview

The Yukaghirs, also called *Yukagirs*, are a Siberian ethnic group living in the Russian Far East, in the basin of the Kolyma River. Tundra Yukaghirs live in the Nizhnekolymsky District of the Sakha Republic, while Taiga Yukaghirs live in the Sakha Republic and Srednekansky District of Magadan Oblast. Yukaghirs also live in the Sakha Republic and Chukotka Autonomous Okrug. Their total number was 1,509 in the 2002 Census, compared with 1,112 in the 1989 Census. They are associated with nomadic and semi-nomadic hunting, reindeer breeding, fishing, shamanism, and two moribund languages.

## Material culture

### Architecture

A Yukaghir house is called a *chum*.

## Music & performance

They mention an epic poem based around crows and list contemporary Yukaghir-related music videos and performances, including works by Irina Duskulova, a concert at the 5th Yukaghir congress on 20 March 2016, and the Yukaghir folk singer Ragtyna Tymkal.

## Festivals & rituals

They describe rituals and taboos connected with elk and deer hunting, and state that Yukaghirs practice dog sacrifice. Alongside Russian Orthodox beliefs, they practice shamanism. The dominant cults concern ancestral spirits and the spirits of Fire, Sun (*Pugu*), Hunting, Earth, and Water. These spirits can protect people or act as their enemies. *Pugu*, the Sun, is described as the highest judge in all disputes. The spirits of the dead go to a place called *Aibidzi*. Every clan had a shaman called an *alma*; after death, every *alma* was treated as a deity, and the body of the dead shaman was dismembered and kept by the clan as relics.

## Foodways

They state that fishing and hunting deer, moose, wild sheep, and sable are traditional activities.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources describe a Yukaghir epic poem based around crows. The sources also refer to online documentation of Kolyma Yukaghir containing tales, songs, and audio materials, and mention contemporary Yukaghir-related recordings and performances.

## Language & religion

The Yukaghir languages form a small family of two closely related languages: Tundra Yukaghir and Kolyma Yukaghir. They are unclassified, and their origin and relationship to other languages remain unknown. Tundra Yukaghir is also known as Northern Yukaghir or *Wadul*; Kolyma Yukaghir is also known as Forest Yukaghir, Southern Yukaghir, or *Odul*. Extinct varieties include Omok and Chuvan, which survived until the 19th century. The languages are regarded as moribund: fewer than 370 people can speak either language according to one account, while another gives 516 people who reported speaking Yukaghir as their native language in 2020–2021. Most Yukaghirs today speak Yakut and Russian. Religious life combines Russian Orthodox beliefs with shamanism.
